name: Grace Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, totally. I like this kind of thing, go for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a contract warehouse, what they call third-party logistics, which means we store and send orders for about forty small online brands. Candles, protein powder, dog treats, phone cases, all in one building by the old railway yard. I pick with a trolley and a handheld, then pack at a bench, and every brand has its own box and its own little thank-you card. Seven till three, five days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety, honestly, no two hours are the same, one minute it's glitter candles, the next it's horse supplements. What wears me out is the pay, lower end, and the peaks when a brand goes viral and we get three thousand orders overnight. I share a house with my cousin and I've got maybe three weeks of savings, because I put most spare money into my side thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the AI stuff I use is handy but it's not magic. I'd post something like, AI writes my listings, it doesn't pack my boxes. At work I'd just say same as ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep doing what I'm doing. I use AI every day for my vintage clothes reselling, it writes the descriptions and suggests prices. If that's all it ever does, fine, it's still saving me two hours a night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse job and keep growing the reselling, it's about £200 a month now. I'd go for the inventory controller job they keep advertising, that's £2 an hour more. And I'd try to keep three weeks' money as a floor, no lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, but upbeat about the side thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the inventory controller job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the person who checks the stock counts match the system and sorts out the mismatches. Mostly a screen job with some walking. Debbie does it now and she's leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put spare money into reselling instead of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because savings at my pay grow by about £30 a month. The reselling grows faster if I buy good stock at car boot sales. It's a risk, I know.

Keep **three weeks** of money as a floor.
feel: **Uneasy** about money but upbeat about her side business.

Use AI each night to write listings and set prices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great for small sellers like me, I can run a little shop like a big one. I'd say warehouses will change slowly. Online I'd post tips on using AI for listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it flips my plan. The inventory controller job is exactly the thinking work AI takes. So the job I wanted is the one that goes first. It's counting and matching on a screen, while picking at a bench full of glitter candles is harder for a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the inventory controller idea and stay on the floor for now. I'd push the reselling harder, maybe sell for other people too, take a cut for doing their listings and photos. And I'd do a short online course on running a shop properly, it's about £60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit thrilled. It's a weird mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the warehouse for the reselling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, not at £200 a month. If it got to about £900 a month steady for six months, then yes. Until then the warehouse is my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your warehouse would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office girls who do customer queries for the brands, the where's-my-parcel emails. That's all going to a chatbot. I'd show them how I use AI, if they want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to move fast. I'd post about it, probably too much. I'd tell everyone at work to learn the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the reselling gets crowded, because everyone will have the same AI and the margins drop. The warehouse gets about three years after 2028 before robots can pack a glitter candle. So I'd have three years of rent money and a side business that might not survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, stop buying stock for a few months and get to six weeks of money. I'd look at something where people pay for a person, maybe styling or running pop-up vintage stalls, because the in-person bit is harder to copy. And I'd keep picking for as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but mostly anxious, because of the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said margins drop. Does that change how you see AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. AI is my friend while I'm ahead. When everyone's got AI, it's just the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stock buying, then the gym, then takeaways. I'd move back to my mum's before I'd go into debt, she's twenty minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something. I'd post about learning the tools and building a side income. I'd say it at work as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI, eight for robots, I'd be 35. That's long enough to grow the reselling into a real small shop, maybe with a market stall. The warehouse becomes my safety net while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to get the reselling to £600 a month by the end of year one. I'd cut my warehouse hours to four days once I'm there. And I'd keep using AI for listings, photos and bookkeeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a hopeful way. I could make this work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm back to full-time picking until the robots come, and that's a worry. Five years is a long time to be wrong about my little shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheap market stall rent and some small business advice that isn't a course trying to sell me another course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so start a side thing now. I'd post that. I'd tell my cousin too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for AGI and about 2039 for the robots, I'd be 40. I'd have a proper shop by then, or I'd have tried and moved on to something else. I'm not too worried, except about money right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop slowly, save £50 a month, keep the warehouse. Maybe in year three rent a small unit. I'd stay in the warehouse until the shop paid more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly the normal money kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good month. If I had three good months in a row, I'd go to four days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think your cousin would cope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. My cousin is at a call centre. A call centre is the first job AI takes. I'd tell her to come and help with the shop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the side business gets crowded at the same time the warehouse clock starts. What would help is cheap space to sell in person, like market stalls, and advice that isn't trying to sell me something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about side jobs. Half the people I pick next to have a side job, nails, food, delivery. That's the real safety net round here, not savings.

headlineQuote: Half the people I pick next to have a side job, nails, food, delivery. That's the real safety net round here, not savings.
portrait: **Grace** is 27, picks and packs for forty brands at a contract warehouse, and shares a house with her cousin.
She has about **three weeks** of savings because spare money goes into her vintage reselling.
She uses **AI daily** for listings and prices, and is curious and comfortable with risk.
She spots that the **screen job** she wanted is more exposed than her floor job.
Her mood stays uneasy to **anxious**, steadied by the side business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her side business crowds out as the **warehouse** clock starts.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **market stall** space and plain small business advice.
